title: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet in Shenzhen in First Three-Way Summit of the World’s Biggest Nuclear Powers
shortdescription: President Donald Trump met Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC, with nuclear arms control, Ukraine and Iran expected on the agenda.
author: Jennifer Albright
seoTitle: Trump, Xi, Putin Meet at APEC in Shenzhen: What to Know

content: President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin came together in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen this week for a meeting that all sides have called historic, billed as the first-ever simultaneous meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers. The talks are taking place on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, which runs November 18-19.

Trump held a bilateral meeting with Putin on Thursday. Chinese state media then reported that the Trump-Xi bilateral had begun at Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort that is also the venue for the three-way session scheduled for later the same day. Official readouts from the Xi meeting and the trilateral had not been released at the time of writing, so this report covers the build-up, the early meetings and what analysts expect.

sections.heading: A Red-Carpet Arrival and a Meeting With Putin
content: Trump reached Shenzhen on Wednesday after an earlier stop in Manila, where he met Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and announced a trade deal. ABC News reported that Xi greeted him personally at the foot of Air Force One, with a red-carpet ceremony, troops, dancers and a five-jet flyover. ABC noted that Xi had not greeted Trump in person at the airport during Trump’s May visit to Beijing. Trump then joined Xi and Putin for an APEC welcome banquet that evening, according to CNBC.

On Thursday, after the leaders’ plenary session, Trump sat down with Putin. Greeting him, Trump said he thought “a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start,” and indicated that a second meeting would follow later, according to a report by the Indian news agency ANI. Trump has also said that meeting Xi and Putin together made sense because the two leaders work together, he told Fox News.

Putin had earlier held his own talks with Xi in Shenzhen. ANI reported that Xi described China-Russia relations as steady and resilient, while Putin said political cooperation between the two countries remained constructive despite a difficult international environment. Nikkei Asia counted the Trump-Xi meeting as their third this year.

sections.heading: Nuclear Arms Control Tops Trump’s Stated Agenda
content: Trump has made denuclearization the centerpiece of what he says he wants from the summit. White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said he would discuss reducing nuclear weapons, according to Defense News. Beijing has confirmed the meeting and described it as being of “groundbreaking significance,” NBC News reported, but it has not said arms control is on the agenda. Foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said only that the three leaders would exchange views on world peace and strategic stability.

The backdrop is stark. New START, the last US-Russia strategic arms treaty, expired in February 2026, leaving the two countries without numerical limits on their arsenals for the first time since 1972, Defense News reported. The United States and Russia each hold roughly 4,000 nuclear weapons in their stockpiles. China was never party to New START and is estimated to have the third-largest arsenal, at several hundred warheads, though analysts believe it is expanding fast. The Atlantic Council’s Alyxandra Marine said China is projected to exceed 1,000 warheads by 2030 and has so far refused trilateral talks, citing the gap in size.

Trump has acknowledged the difficulty, telling Fox News that cutting stockpiles would be hard for all three countries. Other topics expected to come up include the Iran conflict, global trade and Russia’s war in Ukraine, ANI reported. A South China Morning Post report cited by Defense News said working-level teams had discussed artificial intelligence in critical weapons systems, a subject one source described as an easy deliverable.

sections.heading: Experts Expect Symbolism Over Substance
content: Analysts at the Atlantic Council said the agenda is fluid and expect few concrete results. Melanie Hart, a former State Department China adviser, said Xi wants to showcase his convening power ahead of the 2027 Party Congress, where he could win an unprecedented fourth term, and that Beijing is scripting the event closely. John Herbst, a former US ambassador to Ukraine, argued that Putin wants an arrangement in which great powers settle the fate of smaller nations such as Ukraine. Andrew Peek said Trump, whose meeting was arranged on short notice, is focused on optics and precedent and will likely raise Iran, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

On nuclear issues, Nikita Degtyarev of the Open Nuclear Network told Defense News that the most likely outcome is a restatement of the Reagan-Gorbachev principle that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, since there was not enough time for officials to negotiate anything more substantive. Heather Williams of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said any nuclear outcome would probably be a political statement rather than a verifiable, binding agreement. Some Russian commentators have framed the meeting as “Yalta 2.0,” a comparison Degtyarev called overblown.

sections.heading: Ukraine and Allies Watch From Outside the Room
content: No Ukrainian or European representatives are at the table. Dhruva Jaishankar of the Observer Research Foundation America said the absence of key stakeholders raises doubts about what the talks can achieve on ending the war in Ukraine. The Atlantic Council’s Myroslava Gongadze said Ukrainians fear becoming a bargaining chip in a new great-power order, while Daniel Fried said Europeans worry about deals struck over their heads. Rick Hoehne said East Asian allies fear abandonment, with Taiwan concerned about suspended arms sales, Japan about Russia-China alignment and the Philippines about South China Sea disputes.

In Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his team would receive briefings from US representatives on Trump’s discussions in China and coordinate next steps with European leaders on November 19, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

sections.heading: What to Watch Next
content: The key questions are whether the leaders issue any joint or parallel statement on nuclear risk reduction or the use of AI in nuclear command and control, whether the second Trump-Putin meeting Trump alluded to takes place, and whether the talks produce any movement on Ukraine or Iran. Until official readouts are released, claims about outcomes from any side should be treated with caution.

title: Trump Weighs New Strikes on Iran as Netanyahu Presses for a Joint Four-to-Seven-Day Air Campaign
shortdescription: The New York Times reports President Trump is weighing another round of extensive strikes on Iran, but no decision has been made as Israel lobbies Washington to join a short air campaign.
author: Kenneth M. Butts
seoTitle: Trump Weighs New Iran Strikes as Israel Presses for Air Campaign

content: President Donald Trump is weighing another round of extensive military strikes on Iran but has not made a decision, The New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing US and Israeli officials briefed on the discussions. According to the report, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressing Washington to join Israel in a four- to seven-day air campaign against the Islamic Republic.

Trump has signalled publicly that action is not imminent. Axios reported that he indicated on Wednesday that a strike was not around the corner, and the Times of Israel reported that he suggested it might not happen until after the new year. None of the reporting says an order has been given.

sections.heading: The Intelligence Behind the Push
content: Israeli officials have told their American counterparts that Iran has rebuilt its missile and drone arsenals and is advancing chemical and biological weapons programs, according to summaries of the Times report. Netanyahu sent Mossad director Roman Gofman to Washington last week, where he met CIA Director John Ratcliffe, and Israel’s military intelligence chief, Shlomi Binder, has argued with US counterparts for resuming operations.

Trump told Fox News on Wednesday that there were indications Iran was exploring chemical and biological weapons. The Times of Israel reported that some US officials believe the Israeli presentation was “agenda driven.” Axios quoted a statement saying Trump has all options at his disposal to ensure Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.

sections.heading: An Administration Divided, and a Political Cost
content: Officials in the Trump administration disagree about how strong the intelligence is and whether striking Iran again is wise, according to the Times report as summarized by investingLive. The same summary says Trump is also weighing the significant US firepower now in the region, which may not stay there indefinitely.

There is a political price to weigh. Voters signalled unhappiness with the war at this month’s midterm elections, citing higher prices and the lack of the quick victory promised at the outset, according to the same summary. Netanyahu’s own position is described as fragile after Israel’s elections last month, and Axios reported that he is lobbying Trump to go back to war as soon as possible. Leaders of Gulf countries, which fear a devastating Iranian response, are urging Trump to resist and keep tightening economic pressure instead, Axios said.

sections.heading: Strain Inside Iran
content: Iran shows no sign of making concessions, Reuters reported on November 16, but its own warnings about winter gas shortages point to vulnerabilities. Reuters said the war began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and that Iran’s ports are now blockaded.

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said this winter’s shortfall will likely reach 430 million cubic metres, compared with 300 million last year, after four gas processing plants were damaged early in the war. A senior Iranian source told Reuters that Tehran is in talks to import gas from Russia. Two Iranian officials said the leadership is increasingly worried about public unrest; one described the hardship as a fire “smouldering beneath ashes.” Analyst Saeed Leylaz called the pressure the most severe siege Iran has faced since the revolution.

sections.heading: Oil and Energy Markets on Edge
content: Oil prices rose on Thursday, partly on the Times report, investingLive said. A loaded tanker was also struck by an unidentified projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, adding to supply worries. The strait carried about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas before the war, and the Associated Press reported in August that Iran had largely closed it.

International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol said in April that the war was causing the biggest energy crisis in history, and the Times of Israel’s live blog on Thursday carried a fresh item on an agency warning that the Iran crisis poses the largest threat to energy security ever.

sections.heading: What to Watch
content: Iran is also expected to come up at the Trump-Xi-Putin talks in Shenzhen, where Atlantic Council analyst Andrew Peek expects Trump to raise reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The next signals to watch are any formal decision from the White House, further Israeli lobbying, the Gulf states’ response and whether Iran’s winter fuel crisis changes Tehran’s calculations.

title: Ukraine Turns to Allies’ Meeting After Abu Dhabi Talks Yield Prisoner Swap but No Breakthrough
shortdescription: Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large prisoner exchange, but disputes over territory, European troops and Europe’s seat at the table keep a peace deal out of reach.
author: Antonio M. Davis
seoTitle: Ukraine Talks: Prisoner Swap Agreed, No Breakthrough on Peace

content: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a large prisoner-of-war exchange, but a week after US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi the two sides remain far apart on territory, security guarantees and who gets a seat at the negotiating table. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that his team would hold talks with representatives of President Donald Trump on November 19, alongside a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing of European leaders, which the Kyiv Independent reported is being held in Berlin, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

Zelenskyy said Kyiv would use the meetings to coordinate next steps in the negotiations with Russia, receive briefings on Trump’s discussions in China, and prepare new support packages for defence and for the energy sector. He told the Kyiv Independent the main aim in Berlin is to secure more support for Ukraine’s air defenses and energy sector.

sections.heading: What Abu Dhabi Produced
content: The Associated Press reported that the Abu Dhabi talks, held on Tuesday and Wednesday of last week, were the first direct meeting between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in nine months. The session lasted about four hours on Tuesday and just under two hours on Wednesday, and ended with no major breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year-old full-scale invasion.

The one concrete result was an agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange. US envoy Jared Kushner called it the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners so far, and Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky and Ukraine’s delegation lead Rustem Umerov confirmed it. Final numbers have not been announced. A Russian General Staff official, Alexander Zorin, said the swap could take place within two to three weeks. Zelenskyy later described it as a real result.

Both sides described the talks positively. Medinsky said they helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, and Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov called them substantive and useful. Kushner was more guarded, saying there was “no trust right now” between the sides.

sections.heading: Kremlin and Dublin
content: On Thursday, November 12, Kushner and Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin for about two hours, then flew to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy for more than an hour, according to the AP. Zelenskyy was in the Irish capital for a gathering of more than 40 European countries that included NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Putin’s positions did not soften. He told the envoys that any European troops deployed to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be unacceptable and would be treated as legitimate targets, and that the war would resume immediately, the AP reported. He also reminded them of Moscow’s 2021 demands that NATO roll back deployments in Central and Eastern Europe, and Russia says a peace deal should treat its border with Ukraine as extending to four Ukrainian regions it annexed in 2022 but does not fully control.

sections.heading: The Fight Over Europe’s Role
content: A central question is whether Europe joins the talks. Kushner said one goal of the Moscow trip was to win Putin’s approval for European representatives to take part in discussions on the continent’s broader security arrangements, and Witkoff said the Europeans would join at the next meeting without saying which countries would attend. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Europe must first name a representative, and the United States and Ukraine want Europe to choose a single negotiator. Russia objects to European participation because Europe funds and arms Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said Europe would be part of the negotiating team rather than a separate track, and that Europeans would have a voice, according to Anadolu Agency. The Kremlin did not confirm that Putin agreed to include Europe. Some analysts say Washington may be willing to grant Russia concessions on NATO strategy in return for peace, a prospect that alarms European leaders, the AP reported. Last month, Trump waived sanctions and approved a deal to import Russian diesel, a move that angered Kyiv and Europe.

sections.heading: The War Continues on the Ground and in the Sky
content: Fighting continues along a front line of about 1,200 kilometres. Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities have disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies, which Kyiv calls the weaponization of winter. In the overnight attack before the Kremlin meeting, Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered, hitting 17 locations, while Russia’s Defense Ministry said it downed 71 Ukrainian drones.

Zelenskyy also said Ukraine’s military is facing another slowdown of SpaceX’s Starshield service, which it uses to intercept drones and conduct strikes, and that a military investigation found the restrictions were not random errors. Elon Musk acknowledged last month that SpaceX had throttled Starlink in Ukraine for about a week, saying it could not be used for offensive strikes on Russia. On Wednesday, the Kyiv Independent reported that Kyiv says Ukrainian drones hit two Russian oil refineries in Krasnodar Krai.

sections.heading: A Parallel Summit in Shenzhen
content: The Kyiv meetings coincide with the Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen, where Ukraine is not represented. Analysts quoted by the Atlantic Council and ANI have warned that Ukrainians risk becoming a bargaining chip in a new great-power order. Zelenskyy has said that “Russia will achieve none of its objectives,” the Kyiv Independent reported. Whether the next round of talks includes Europe, and whether the prisoner swap goes ahead on schedule, will show how much momentum the diplomacy really has.

title: Bank Indonesia Raises Benchmark Rate to 6% in Pre-Emptive Move to Defend the Rupiah
shortdescription: Bank Indonesia lifted its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 6 percent, citing rupiah stability and expectations of further US Federal Reserve rate increases.
author: Arthur A. Johnson
seoTitle: Bank Indonesia Hikes Rate to 6% to Defend Rupiah Amid Fed Fears

content: Bank Indonesia raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6 percent on Wednesday, November 18, calling the move pre-emptive and aimed at keeping Indonesian assets attractive and stabilising the rupiah as the US Federal Reserve may raise rates again, Antara News reported. The decision followed the board’s two-day meeting on November 17-18.

The central bank also raised its deposit facility rate to 5.25 percent and its lending facility rate to 6.75 percent. Antara said the latest move brings cumulative increases in 2026 to 125 basis points.

sections.heading: A Surprise to Many Forecasters
content: The decision was not what most forecasters expected. In a poll of 38 respondents cited by BatamNewsAsia, 22 expected Bank Indonesia to hold the rate at 5.75 percent, while 16 anticipated a 25-basis-point increase. BatamNewsAsia described it as the central bank’s first increase since June.

sections.heading: Why Bank Indonesia Moved
content: Governor Destry Damayanti said the increase was intended to further strengthen rupiah stabilisation against rising global uncertainty and to keep inflation within its target range, according to Katadata’s Databoks. The central bank’s inflation target is 2.5 percent, plus or minus 1 percentage point, for 2026 and 2027.

Investortrust reported that the rupiah has depreciated 9.35 percent so far this year amid persistent foreign capital outflows, ahead of anticipated Fed rate increases in December 2026 and in 2027. The expectation of tighter US policy has been building. Reuters reported on November 10 that Deutsche Bank expects a Fed rate hike in January 2027 after hot US inflation data.

Senior Deputy Governor Aida S. Budiman said Bank Indonesia expects the Fed to raise rates once more before the end of the year and then pause in 2027. She cautioned that this outlook depends on incoming data, and that if developments threaten Bank Indonesia’s inflation projections, it would consider using the policy rate again.

sections.heading: The Rupiah and the Inflation Picture
content: The rupiah closed at 18,245 per US dollar on November 17, down 0.66 percent from the end of October, according to Databoks. Bank Indonesia attributed the weakness to persistently high global uncertainty and to sentiment among foreign investors in the stock market. The central bank had held its benchmark rate at 5.75 percent in October. Databoks’ market ticker showed consumer inflation at 3.23 percent year on year in October, inside the central bank’s target band.

sections.heading: Beyond the Policy Rate
content: Destry stressed that tightening is part of a broader policy mix rather than a single tool. Asking whether raising interest rates alone would be sufficient, she said the bank is also using unconventional measures, including incentives to lower hedging costs and encourage foreign capital inflows, Antara reported.

According to Databoks, those measures include incentives for swap instruments and for purchases of domestic non-deliverable forward (DNDF) hedging contracts from Bank Indonesia, as well as for local currency transactions with partner countries. The aim is to keep rupiah assets attractive, draw foreign portfolio inflows and deepen the money and foreign exchange markets. Domestic hedging transactions since the policy began in June 2026 had reached about 14.10 billion US dollars as of November 17.

sections.heading: Growth and Credit Outlook
content: Budiman said the rate increase would not necessarily derail economic growth, according to Tempo. Bank Indonesia projects 2026 growth of between 4.9 and 5.7 percent, and bank lending grew 13.21 percent year on year in October.

The central bank’s next decisions will depend on how the Fed moves in December and on whether rupiah pressure eases. For households and businesses, higher benchmark rates typically feed through to loan and deposit rates over time, though the pace depends on how quickly commercial banks adjust.

title: Pope Leo XIV Ends 12-Day South America Tour With Farewell Mass for 1.5 Million in Lima
shortdescription: Pope Leo XIV closed his first South America tour as pontiff in Peru, the country he calls his homeland, weeks after lung cancer surgery.
author: Hope M. Pender
seoTitle: Pope Leo Ends South America Tour With Mass for 1.5 Million
primaryKeyword: Pope Leo XIV South America tour
secondaryKeywords: Pope Leo Peru farewell Mass Lima

content: Pope Leo XIV ended a 12-day, three-nation tour of South America on Monday, November 16, with a farewell Mass in Lima before an estimated 1.5 million people, Reuters reported. He then flew from Lima to Rome that afternoon, Vatican News reported, closing the first South American trip of his papacy.

The tour began on November 6 in Uruguay and moved on to Argentina and Peru. It came less than a month after Leo had surgery for lung cancer in Rome on October 13, according to the Associated Press. Reuters reported that he appeared in good form throughout, delivering long speeches in a firm voice and coping with strong winds in Uruguay and with altitude and heat in Peru.

Crowd estimates varied. Reuters said the trip, which included about 50 events, drew a record 13 million people in total, while the Buenos Aires Herald cited an official estimate of more than six million.

sections.heading: A Homecoming in Peru
content: Peru was the most personal leg. Born in Chicago, Leo spent about two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, served as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, and holds both US and Peruvian citizenship. He called Peru his homeland and sang the national anthem with President Keiko Fujimori, the AP reported. His arrival in Lima on November 11 drew about 3 million people, according to the Vatican, the largest event of his 18-month papacy and the biggest papal gathering since 2015, Reuters said.

On Sunday, November 15, he travelled from Chiclayo to Cusco, at about 11,150 feet, then to Pucallpa in the Amazon, and back to Lima, the AP reported. He also visited the Mogrovejo sanctuary in Zaña, in the Chiclayo diocese, where he had prayed the night before his ordination as bishop. On his last day he visited a home for the elderly in Callao, run by the Little Sisters of the Abandoned Elderly, and told residents “hasta pronto, hasta luego,” or see you soon, according to the AP.

sections.heading: A Homily Built Around a Peruvian Saint
content: In his homily at the final Mass, Leo spoke of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo, a Spanish layman and lawyer who became the second archbishop of Lima. According to America magazine, Leo described him walking hundreds of kilometres to reach Indigenous communities, learning local languages, pressing for the ordination of Indigenous people and mestizos, and giving generously to the poor. Leo said Peru needs more “oases of fraternity” and fewer “deserts of individualism,” and urged priests, religious, families and volunteers to serve the poor and the marginalised. Earlier that day, he visited the Little Sisters’ home for the elderly in Callao, which he called an “oasis of dignity.”

sections.heading: Messages to Political Leaders
content: The tour carried political messages. In Argentina, the homeland of the late Pope Francis, who never returned there as pope, Leo urged President Javier Milei not to target the country’s poorest with austerity measures, Reuters reported. The Church has criticised cuts to social services. In Peru, he called on Fujimori to build public confidence after her narrow election victory earlier this year.

sections.heading: A Call to Protect the Amazon
content: In Pucallpa, at the eastern edge of the Amazon, Leo condemned the exploitation of the rainforest and urged Catholics to oppose deforestation and pollution “with perseverance,” Reuters reported. Members of the Shipibo-Konibo Indigenous people performed a traditional dance during a meeting with Amazonian communities at Malecón Puerto Callao in Pucallpa on November 15, according to America magazine’s coverage of the trip.

sections.heading: Meetings With Abuse Survivors
content: Leo met five survivors of clergy sexual abuse in Argentina and six in Peru. The Vatican said that in Peru he discussed how the Church can better listen to victims. Some survivors criticised the small size of the groups, and victims staged a small protest outside the Vatican embassy in Lima, Reuters reported. Abuse survivor José Escardó said many victims hoped the pope would look them in the eyes and listen.

sections.heading: A Farewell, With No New Announcements
content: At the end of the Mass at Las Palmas Air Base, Leo told Peruvians he wanted to confirm them in faith and charity and assured them, “I will always carry you with me,” America magazine reported. He added that the Peruvian people are his people too, and the crowd applauded and chanted that he is Peruvian.

Vatican News reported that he said Peru taught him to be a bishop and helped him better understand his role as Successor of Peter, and that the songs, dances and incense had renewed his conviction that the mission must reach the ends of the earth. His plane left Callao Air Base at 2:28 p.m. local time and was due to land at Rome’s Fiumicino Airport on Tuesday morning. The trip produced no new Church policy announcements, according to Reuters.

Residents in Chiclayo described the visit as bittersweet, since he may not return soon. America magazine’s Vatican correspondent, Gerard O’Connell, called the trip “extraordinarily successful” and said Leo’s heart is clearly in Peru.
